title: Fifteen Counts
blurb: A stuck cage, a worn cable and one rescue Pin give Dagny fifteen counts to spend, and the league's next notice leaves her nowhere to hide.

blocks.text: I put my right foot on the first rung of the Shaft Nine ladder at first light, and my knee would not lift me.

I took the rail in my right hand and pulled. My thigh shook. The knee bent and stayed bent, and the rest of me did not come up after it. I pulled harder and got my left boot onto the rung beside the right, and that was all. I could not go up, and when I tried to step back down the knee would not take me down either. I stood on one iron rung with my face against the cold rail and could not move.

I had counted the weeks on the kitchen floor all night. A stone a week since the Coopers, an ounce an hour, near enough, and the hours since Coldhithe had carried me over the line while I sat there. Six stone and a pound of lean-weight in my bones. The Weighman's book would still say four, because I had registered heavy and nobody had checked. My knee did not read the book. Heavy, the league calls it: an Anchor who can't climb a stair, a ladder or a rope without help.

Last night I had asked my father to hold the brake. He has been dead two years. Nobody was going to hold it. Somewhere across Scarrow a Weighhouse cage was waiting for my brother on a Weighhouse cable, and the only person who knew what that meant and loved him was standing on the bottom rung of a ladder, stuck.
"Dagny?"
Lisbet's face came over the Lip above me with a coil of rope on her shoulder. She was always up before anyone on the morning after a match, whipping the ends of the fixed ropes.
"I can't come up," I said. "And I can't get down."
She didn't ask why. She threw a bight down to me, came down six rungs above my head and took a turn round the rail. "Arm through. Under the other one. Now off the rail and sit in it."
I sat in it. She lowered me the height of one rung, which was all it was, and I stood on the cinders with my knees shaking and the rope still round me.

"Rafe's gone to Teague," I said. "He's signing onto the deep-lift crew at Shaft Four. Ten years. He's sixteen." My throat shut and I made it open. "I'm frightened for him, Lisbet. I'm frightened he's already signed. And I'm Heavy. I went over in the night. I'm frightened of that too."
She looked at me for a count. Then she coiled the rope over her elbow. "Right. The rope barrow's in the shed. You're riding. Move."

Shaft Four is a working shaft, on the far side of the Weighhouse yard. Lisbet pushed me there in the rope barrow with my legs over the front and my right hand on the side, and every rut in the road went up through my spine and sat in my knees.

The banksman at the pithead knew my father's coat before he knew my face. "Abel's girl," he said, and took his cap off. "Your Rafe went down at six with Mr Teague. Crew landing, then on down in the deep cage to sign at the bottom tally. You'll catch them coming back up."
He let us ride the main cage down. I didn't have to climb into it. I only had to step, and Lisbet held my arm for the step.

The crew landing is a cut in the shaft wall, a hundred metres down, lamplit, with the deep cage's drum and lever at the back of it and the deep shaft going on below its lip into the dark. An old Weighhouse safety rule puts one rescue Pin on every lift landing. Shaft Four's sat in the floor two strides from the lip, iron ring rusty at the edges, and I looked at it the way you look at a doorway in a fire.
The lever-man was Corbet Pye. He had stood that lever twenty years and had walked behind my father's coffin. He had his right wrist strapped.
"Two riders coming up," he said, when the bell rang twice from below. "That's them. Your brother and Teague."
"Let me bring him up, Mr Pye."
He looked at my left hand in my pocket, and at the coat. He knew the gate that took my two fingers had been a cage gate, and he knew whose lever I had stood beside when it happened. He stepped aside.
"Slow at the top," he said. "The guides are worn at the top. She sticks. And go easy on the cable. It's the old one. Two years I've asked them for a new one."
My father asked them too. I put my right hand on the lever and felt the drum take the weight, and I wound.

The cable came up out of the dark with its paint marks on it, one every ten metres, and I counted them in. Nine. Seven. Five. The bell rope trembled. Three. One. The cage roof came up into the lamplight below the lip, and I saw Rafe's face through the bars, white and grinning, and Teague behind him in his grey coat with his hat in his hand.
Then the guide shoe screamed on the worn iron and the cage stopped.
It stopped dead, its floor a long step below the landing, and the cable above it went tight and hummed. Pye was at my shoulder. "Don't wind! Don't wind, she'll part!"

I didn't wind. I held the lever still and heard the cable hum and heard my own breath, and I thought of a cable two years ago that the Weighhouse wouldn't change, and the Settle cage on the end of it, and my father.
"Bit of a queue at the top, is there, Dags?" Rafe's voice came up through the bars, too loud. "Not stopping here all morning, are we?"

The keeps were at the landing, two iron catches on the guides. The cage had to rise a hand and a half to sit on them. It was jammed, and the cable might not take another pull, and if the jam let go the cage would drop onto a cable that might not take that either.

The rescue Pin's zone runs from a metre below the landing to seven above it. The cage stood inside it, all of it, and a few metres of cable over it. I did the sum before I knew I was doing it. A man-cage and its cable, about two heads. Rafe, one. Teague, a big man, one and a half. About four heads, near enough. Set it straight up and it costs four stone a minute. A stone every fifteen counts.

I was six stone and a pound in my bones. At ten a bone cracks, the foot first, and my left foot had been aching since Coldhithe. That was a minute. And more than four stone in one hold, let go any way at all, would put a second lean on me and double what the first one was costing. I had fifteen counts to spend. Twenty, if it went wrong.
"Mr Pye, Lisbet, off the landing. Into the drift, out of the shaft." They went. I raised my voice. "Rafe! Mr Teague! Both hands on the roof bars and hold on. You're going to fall up."
"Up, is it?" Rafe said. "Course we are." But his hands went up. Teague dropped his hat and his went up too.

I walked the two strides to the Pin. They were the longest two strides of my life, and my knees said so on every one. I went down onto one knee, because I couldn't bend any other way, and I put my right hand on the ring and gripped it.
One count before it would turn. I felt the shaft come into my hand.

Then I turned it. A quarter-turn every three counts, smooth, and no faster for wanting. At three counts the cage's down was sideways and the cage ground against the guides and I heard Teague grunt. At six it pointed straight up.
They fell. Rafe and Teague went up off the floor and hit the roof bars with their backs, and the whole cage lifted. The guide shoe shrieked once and came free. The cable went slack in loops above it.
The weight came into me.

It came in through my knees first, and then the hips, and then the left foot, which had been a cup with a crack in it since Coldhithe and now felt like it was holding more water than it could. My right hand was locked on the ring. I could not feel the floor under my knee, only the press of everything above it. Seven counts. Eight. The cage rose past the lip, slow, the roof first, then the bars, then Rafe's boots hanging up toward the roof.
"Cage coming up, Da," I said, into the ring. "Hold the brake."
Eleven. Twelve. The keeps clacked as the cage floor went by them. Thirteen. They clacked again and dropped into place underneath.
I did the Release the way Osk taught me. I breathed in all the way, and felt the Pin go quiet in my hand, and let the breath and the hand go together, little finger last.
True down came back. The cage dropped a finger's width onto the keeps with a bang that went up the shaft, and Rafe and Teague came down off the roof onto the floor in a heap.

Fifteen counts. One stone. Seven stone and a pound in my bones, two stone thirteen from a cracked foot. Off plumbstone, ordinary carry drains at half the rate, so a stone wants eight hours lying flat, and it would be gone before Monday. I said all that to myself on my knee on the landing, and then I sat down where I was, because there was nothing in my legs.
Pye ran the gate back. Rafe came out first, on his hands, then on his feet, and stood there looking at me and didn't say anything at all, which is how I know he is frightened past joking.
"Lisbet," I said. "Take him to the main cage. I want a word with Mr Teague."
"Move, Rafe," Lisbet said, and took him by the collar, and he went.

I got myself to the cage gate on my hands and sat in it, across the threshold, my back on one post and my boots on the other. Teague was inside, standing, brushing the roof dirt off his coat. He picked up his hat. He didn't try to step over me.
"Thank you, Dagny Quillon," he said. "That was very exact."

"Wat Ellery walked out an hour before the bell," I said. "In new boots. Boots like that cost a month of a miner's pay. Pru Ambry wrote my brother's slip at fours, on your order, when the gate board had us at two. The back of every slip voids a match with an unregistered player in it. You knew there'd be one. You'd paid for there to be one."
He turned his hat round once in his hands. Below us the shaft was quiet. The cable ticked as it cooled.
"You do add up," he said.
"Say it."

"I paid Wat Ellery to walk out. I had Pru Ambry take your brother's bet at a price that would bring him in, and I knew the clause would void it, and the eighty crowns would still be owed." He said it the way he says interest, to the day. "The Weighhouse pays me for every able Anchor I bring under contract. Head-money. An able girl who tested at fourteen and never signed, young, untrained, is worth three times the usual."
"My father refused it for me."

"Your father always knew what a cage weighed," Teague said. "He weighed everything he sent down, and he weighed you at fourteen and wouldn't send you. I needed something heavier to put on the other side. Your brother's paper is worth nothing to me on its own, a lift-crew boy. But it brought you to the lever, didn't it? I'd have offered it to you this morning, torn, for your name on an Anchor contract. A contracted Anchor's family debts are bought by the Weighhouse."
My hands had gone cold in the coat lining. I made them stay still.
"I just brought you up on a cable they won't change," I said. "The same as the one that dropped my father."
"Yes," he said. "I thought of that. At the bottom."
"Then you owe me a life, Mr Teague, and I'm calling it in. Give me his paper."
"And if I keep it?"

"Then I say at the Lip that you paid a Ninepins Anchor to walk out and void your own book. Every man in Scarrow whose stake you kept under that clause will want it back. Pru Ambry will say it. Dunnet Haig will say what you paid him for. And the Weighhouse won't want its head-money man known for it."
He was quiet a long time. Then he said, very softly, "It would be a shame, Dagny Quillon."
"It would. Give me the paper."

He took it out of his inside pocket. Rafe's name was on it in Rafe's hand, the big R he has made since he was six. It hadn't gone to the clerk yet. I held one edge in my right hand and the other between the thumb and first finger of my left, the two that still close, and I tore it across, and across again, and put the pieces in my coat.
"I'll not say it at any Lip," I said. "Not while that stays torn."
"A hundred and four today," Teague said, and put his hat on. "A hundred and twelve on the day of the Step. I'll be at the Lip."

Lisbet and Rafe got me into the main cage between them. The banksman rang it up. It is a long ride, a hundred metres, and the lamps went past one by one, and Rafe stood against the bars with his hands in his pockets and didn't look at me.
"I signed, Dags," he said at last. Very still. Very plain. "In the book at the bottom. They showed me where I'd work. It's wet down there, and dark, and I signed anyway, didn't I?"
"It's torn," I said. "It's in my pocket."
"That Pin cost you."
"A stone. My left foot is aching with it."
He looked at me then. He wanted to say something about it, and he looked at Lisbet, and didn't.
I hadn't said it to him since he was small. I said it now, with the lamps going past, because I had nearly watched him drop down a shaft on a worn cable and I would not have that between us unsaid.
"I love you, Rafe."
His face did something I hadn't seen since our father's funeral. "You never say that."
"I'm saying it. You're not a weight I carry. You're my brother."
He put his face against the bars. Lisbet looked at the wall of the shaft going down past us and pretended to count the lamps.

They winched me up to the Shaft Nine Lip that evening in the sling, the way they winch Osk's chair: Dunnet on the handle, Lisbet calling the turns. I had lain flat on the kitchen floor all afternoon and it had taken a good part of the stone off. It had taken none of the six.

The whole team was there. Hal stood by the rail with his hand on his strapped side. Osk sat in his chair with the grit ringing its legs. Pru had her book open and wouldn't meet Rafe's eye, and I knew from that she hadn't told him yet.
The Weighman came at seven, with the league book under his arm, to read the table.

"Shaft League, Thaw Round, final," he said. "Tallymen, first. Ninepins, second." Dunnet let out a breath that was half a laugh. "Ninepins to play the Step against the Blackwick Colliers, seventh in the Seam League, Monday next."
Rafe grabbed my good arm and shook it. I let him.

Then the Weighman opened the book and turned the pages slowly, and stopped on one, and I knew whose. Seven Mondays. Seven readings. Each one heavier. His finger rested on the margin, where he had made the small pencil mark by my name, and he didn't look up.

"I've a notice to read," he said. "The league gives notice of an inspection a match ahead, so no family is frightened off the plumbing. Every Anchor of a promoted side will stand under the plumb-bob at the Lip the moment the Step ends. An Anchor found leaning is struck off the register. Match fees and purse share owed to that Anchor are forfeit to the league. An Anchor who refuses the inspection, misses it, or walks away from it is treated as found leaning. An Anchor who withdraws from the register before it forfeits the same, and doesn't play the Step."
He closed the book.

The purse share and my fees were the debt. The debt was Rafe. I could not refuse and I could not withdraw and I could not walk away, and I could not stand under a plumb-bob, because a plumb-bob tilts toward me from a metre off and every Anchor on that Lip would see it. My throat closed. The cold came into my hands, in the coat lining, and stayed. Osk, in his chair, did not turn his head.
I had one match left to stop leaning, and the only way I knew was the one Osk had forbidden me ever to do in front of a Weighman.
The Weighman's eyes came up from the book and stopped on me. Rafe, who did not know, felt my arm go still under his hand and leaned close.
"He means somebody else, doesn't he, Dags?"
